title: A neuron, at rest.
intro: Before a neuron sends a signal, it holds a quiet electrical difference across its membrane.
In this model, that resting potential is −65 millivolts; without an input, the voltage stays there.

symbols.meaning: The membrane’s current electrical potential, in mV.
The resting level: −65 mV in this teaching model.

terms.definition: The boundary that holds the voltage difference.
The external drive into our model neuron, measured in nanoamps.
The output path that carries the neuron’s signal away from its cell body.

predict.question: With no input, what happens to a neuron at rest?
predict.why: At rest with I = 0, both the input and the voltage difference from rest are zero. There is no net change, so the model remains at −65 mV.

challenge.text: Set input to 0 nA and watch the voltage and spike count.

figure_caption: A quiet neuron. Input arrives from the left; the membrane holds its resting potential.

source.title: A single leaky neuron: demonstration notes

learning.objective: Understand why zero input leaves the voltage at rest.
learning.action: Set input to 0 nA and watch the voltage and spike count.
learning.observe: The membrane stays at −65 mV and the spike count stays zero.
learning.mechanism: At rest, input and leak cancel to zero, so the voltage derivative is zero.

title: An input becomes a voltage.
intro: A steady input raises the membrane potential, but the charge also leaks away.
The balance approaches a new resting level; the time constant controls how quickly it gets there.

symbols.meaning: Input current, in nA; the resistance R is fixed at 10 MΩ.
Time constant, in ms: a larger value means a slower response.

terms.definition: The tendency for the membrane voltage to move back toward rest.
Input and leak together determine how voltage changes over time.
A constant current pushes the voltage toward Vrest + RI.
The output path that carries the neuron’s signal away from its cell body.

predict.question: What happens when you make the time constant larger?
options: The voltage reaches its new level faster.
The voltage approaches the same level more slowly.
predict.why: The time constant divides the voltage’s rate of change. A larger τ slows the approach, while the equilibrium Vrest + RI remains the same. With 1 nA and R = 10 MΩ, that equilibrium is −55 mV.

challenge.text: Set input to 1 nA and watch voltage approach its subthreshold equilibrium.

figure_caption: Incoming current and membrane leakage compete. Change τ to feel the difference in pace.

source.title: A single leaky neuron: demonstration notes

learning.objective: See input and leak compete, and τ control response speed.
learning.action: Set input to 1 nA and watch voltage approach its subthreshold equilibrium.
learning.observe: Voltage rises toward −55 mV without reaching the −50 mV threshold.
learning.mechanism: RI=10 mV balances the membrane leak when the voltage is 10 mV above rest.

title: A threshold changes everything.
intro: When the membrane reaches −50 mV, our model emits a spike and resets to −65 mV.
A two-millisecond refractory interval follows, then the membrane begins integrating again.

symbols.meaning: Firing threshold, in mV: cross it to emit a spike.
Reset voltage, in mV, held during the 2 ms refractory interval.

terms.definition: The voltage at which the model emits a spike: −50 mV.
A discrete output event, drawn as a sharp line in the trace.
After a spike, voltage returns to −65 mV before integration resumes.

predict.question: Will a steady input of 1 nA trigger a spike?
options: No: it settles below the firing threshold.
predict.why: An input of 1 nA approaches −55 mV, below the −50 mV threshold. Inputs greater than 1.5 nA can reach the threshold in this model. The spike marker at +20 mV is a drawing convention, not a biological action-potential waveform.

challenge.text: Set input to 2 nA and observe the reset events in the voltage trace.

figure_caption: A voltage trace reveals the threshold, each spike, and the reset that follows it.

source.title: A single leaky neuron: demonstration notes

learning.objective: Connect the threshold crossing to a discrete output spike.
learning.action: Set input to 2 nA and observe the reset events in the voltage trace.
learning.observe: Voltage ramps to −50 mV, then resets; spikes accumulate in the first-second count.
learning.mechanism: After each threshold crossing, the model resets to −65 mV and holds for 2 ms.

title: More input. A faster rhythm.
intro: Stronger input shortens the journey to threshold, so the neuron fires more often.
Our simulation produced 33 spikes at 2 nA and 63 spikes at 3 nA in the first 1 s (0–1000 ms); the tags and the plot count the same window.

symbols.meaning: Approximate steady firing rate. The Firing rhythm tag shows the measured count in the first 1 s.
Input in nA, above 1.5 nA for this expression; R = 10 MΩ.
Time constant in ms; the final 2 ms is the refractory interval.

terms.definition: Spikes counted in the first 1 s (0–1000 ms) of a run, per second.
Time between two spike events; shorter intervals mean a faster rhythm.
The same −50 mV boundary, reached faster under stronger input.

predict.question: Does doubling the input exactly double the firing rate?
options: Yes, the relationship is always linear.
No, threshold and refractory time make it nonlinear.
predict.why: The charging time depends on a logarithm, and every spike adds a refractory interval. Our simulation gives 33 spikes at 2 nA and 63 at 3 nA in the first 1 s (0–1000 ms), matching the checked Python reference. This is numerical agreement with our reference model, not validation against a research paper or biological data. The analytic expression is approximate for the discrete model.

challenge.text: Set input to 3 nA and wait for the first 1,000 ms measurement.

figure_caption: A repeatable result: increase the drive, shorten the intervals, and measure the new rhythm.

source.title: A single leaky neuron: demonstration notes

learning.objective: Compare rates using the same measurement window.
learning.action: Set input to 3 nA and wait for the first 1,000 ms measurement.
learning.observe: The first-second count is 63 spikes, compared with 33 at 2 nA.
learning.mechanism: A stronger input shortens the time to threshold after each reset.
